title: Task Scheduler
prompt: You are given an array of CPU `tasks`, each represented by an uppercase letter, and a non-negative integer `n` representing the cooldown period: the same task can only be run again after at least `n` other units of time have passed (either doing other tasks or being idle). Return the minimum number of time units the CPU needs to finish all the given tasks.

examples.explanation: One valid schedule is A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B, taking 8 time units.
A schedule like A -> B -> C -> D -> A -> B needs no idle time at all.

constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter
hints: Simulating time unit by time unit works but there's a formula based only on the frequency counts.
The most frequent task dictates the overall structure: think of laying out (max_count - 1) 'blocks' of size (n + 1), with the most frequent task anchoring each block.

The answer is max(len(tasks), (max_count - 1) * (n + 1) + number_of_tasks_tied_for_max_count). The first term handles the case where there are enough distinct tasks to fill all the idle slots naturally, making idle time unnecessary.

solution.approach: Count the frequency of each task. Let max_count be the highest frequency and max_count_tasks be how many distinct tasks share that highest frequency. Picture arranging (max_count - 1) full blocks, each of length (n + 1), anchored by one occurrence of a most-frequent task followed by n slots for other tasks or idle time; the final occurrence of the most frequent tasks caps it off, contributing max_count_tasks more slots. This gives a lower bound of (max_count - 1) * (n + 1) + max_count_tasks time units. However, if there are enough other tasks to fill every gap with real work instead of idling, the total simply equals len(tasks). The answer is the maximum of these two quantities.
solution.timeComplexity: O(m) where m is the number of tasks (26-letter alphabet keeps counting O(1) per distinct letter)
